prompt: What's the most reliable test for whether a theme is defensible?
choice_a: You can point to at least three places in the story that support it.
choice_c: Your teacher mentioned it in class.
feedback_a: Correct. A theme is the story's overall claim — it must be supported by multiple details, not just one.
feedback_b: Vocabulary doesn't make a theme defensible.
feedback_c: Authority isn't the test — evidence in the text is.
feedback_d: Drama isn't the test — many real themes are quiet.

prompt: If you can only point to ONE moment in a story to support your theme, what's the most likely problem?
choice_a: The theme is correct but the story is too short.
choice_b: You've picked a plot point and called it a theme. The real theme should be supported across multiple events.
choice_d: The story doesn't have a theme.
feedback_a: Story length isn't usually the issue.
feedback_b: Correct. One supporting moment usually means you grabbed a single scene's lesson instead of the story's overall claim.
feedback_c: Length of the theme statement isn't the issue.
feedback_d: Almost all stories have themes — if you can't find one, you may have picked the wrong claim.

prompt: Read: A family argues at dinner. The teenager stays quiet, takes a walk afterward, and writes a letter the next morning to her grandfather, whom she hasn't spoken to in a year. The grandfather calls back the same day. The story ends with the two of them planning to meet. Which of these themes is BEST supported by the WHOLE story?
choice_a: Reaching out across a long silence is harder, and more worth it, than it seems.
feedback_a: Correct. Supported by the silence (the year), the reaching-out (the letter), the response (the call), and the ending (the plan to meet). Multiple details across the whole story.
feedback_b: Too specific — supported by only one detail (the letter).
feedback_c: Supported by only the dinner scene.
feedback_d: Supported by the walk only — one moment.

prompt: Read: A boy moves to a new town. He meets three new neighbors. The first laughs at his accent. The second invites him to a school event. The third sits with him at lunch. By the end, he says he's starting to feel at home. Which theme is BEST supported?
choice_b: Whether a new place feels like home depends more on the people who welcome you than on the place itself.
feedback_a: Too narrow — only one detail supports this.
feedback_b: Correct. Supported by the three neighbors, the events at school, and the boy's closing observation. Multiple details across multiple characters.
feedback_c: Only two of the three neighbors are nice — the theme has to cover the whole pattern.
feedback_d: Only one moment supports this — a plot detail, not a theme.

prompt: Read: A young runner trains for months. Her coach pushes her. Her parents worry. Her best friend says she's working too hard. On race day, she runs well — and then keeps running for months afterward because she now loves the training, not the medals. Which theme is BEST supported?
choice_c: Sometimes the reasons we start something are not the reasons we end up loving it.
feedback_a: True but too thin — only one element supports it.
feedback_b: Only the coach detail supports this — the parents and friend are different.
feedback_c: Correct. Supported by the training arc (started for medals), the race (success), AND the ending (kept running for love of it). Multiple details, full arc.
feedback_d: A reaction to one detail, not a theme of the whole story.

prompt: Across a story, the same object — say, a worn photograph — appears in three different scenes. What does this most likely signal?
choice_a: The photograph carries meaning beyond itself and is probably part of the theme.
choice_b: The author forgot to remove a detail in editing.
feedback_a: Correct. Recurrence is a classic theme signal. Whatever the photograph stands for (memory, loss, a person, a connection) is probably part of the story's claim.
feedback_b: Authors don't usually leave recurring details by accident.
feedback_c: Three appearances of the same specific object isn't a coincidence — it's emphasis.

prompt: A student picks the theme: "Friendship is important." The story does include friendship — but the student can only point to ONE scene that shows it. What's the better next move?
choice_a: Add more sentences to the theme.
choice_b: Pick a different theme that the student can support with multiple details from across the story.
choice_c: Defend the theme by repeating it more confidently.
choice_d: Look up the answer in a study guide.
feedback_a: Length doesn't fix a weak theme.
feedback_b: Correct. The fix is finding a theme that the story actually supports across multiple scenes — not making the wrong theme longer.
feedback_c: Confidence isn't the test — evidence is.
feedback_d: Study guides don't replace careful reading.

prompt: A story has TWO defensible themes, each supported by different details across the text. What does this most likely indicate?
choice_c: One of the themes must be wrong.
choice_d: Rich stories often carry more than one theme. Both can be correct if both are supported.
feedback_a: Multiple themes are a feature of complex stories, not a sign of confusion.
feedback_b: Length isn't the issue; thematic depth is what's being noticed.
feedback_c: Not necessarily — both can coexist if both are supported.
feedback_d: Correct. Most full-length stories support several themes simultaneously. A defensible answer for a single question usually picks the one BEST supported, but both can exist.

prompt: Read: An older sister teaches her younger brother to ride a bike. He falls, gets back up, falls again. The next week, she teaches him a card trick. He gets it wrong twice. The week after, she teaches him to tie a knot. He gets it on the first try. Which theme is best supported BY THE WHOLE PATTERN, not by any single scene?
choice_b: Card tricks are easier than bicycles.
choice_c: Some skills come faster than others, but the teacher who keeps showing up is what makes any of them possible.
feedback_a: True but too generic — doesn't engage with the specific pattern of three teaching attempts.
feedback_c: Correct. Supported by all three teaching moments — different skills, different difficulty, but the consistent teaching presence is the through-line. The pattern IS the theme.
feedback_d: A generalization about siblings, but supported only loosely by this specific story.

prompt: A student writes a beautiful-sounding theme that's only supported by the story's final sentence. Which is the better critique?
choice_b: The theme uses words that are too easy.
choice_c: The student didn't read the title.
choice_d: Beauty doesn't make a theme defensible — the theme needs to be supported across multiple details, not just one ending line.
feedback_c: The title might help but doesn't fix the support problem.
feedback_d: Correct. The whole skill of A1.2 is that theme requires multiple supporting details. A beautiful theme that's only supported by one line is still under-supported.
